newsitem.title: CYPRUS: OPEC supplies to dominate long-term - analysts.
newsitem.headline: OPEC supplies to dominate long-term - analysts.

text.p: Oil output from OPEC countries will increase after the turn of the century to supply more than half the world's needs, oil analysts said on Monday.
But one of them said OPEC nations found it increasingly difficult to follow quotas imposed to inject stability in world markets when non-member countries were producing at full steam.
"Reduction in OPEC output in order to stabilise oil prices has led to costly capacity non-utilisation," OPEC official Ibrahim Ismail told an oil conference which opened in Cyprus on Monday.
"It is time...that this burden is fairly and equitably shared by both sides," he said.
Ismail, head of the OPEC Energy Section, said production quotas had had a serious impact on revenues, while non-OPEC countries were producing full out.
OPEC wellhead crude output in September was virtually unchanged at 25.86 million barrels per day (bpd) from a revised 25.87 million in August, according to a Reuters survey issued on Monday.
Iraq's prolonged absence from world markets, following the postponement of May's U.N. oil-for-food deal, leaves tight markets without an expected 600,000 bpd of extra fourth quarter supply.
Ismail said most OPEC members were overburdened with debts and budget deficits.
"They are borrowing money from abroad to offset these deficits and their assets abroad, if any, are eroding with time."
Ismail said he expected non-OPEC supply to continue growing until the turn of the century, but later slow down, which will enable OPEC members to increase their share of the market.
World demand growth in 2000 is expected to reach 1.8 million bpd, with OPEC countries supplying 61 percent of it and non-OPEC countries 39 percent, Ismael said.
In 1998 demand is forecast at 1.6 million bpd, with an 88 percent market share to non-OPEC countries and 12 percent to OPEC countries.
"After 2000 I see OPEC getting the market share, between 50 and 58 percent of supply by the year 2010," said Michael Williams of the Paris-based International Energy Agency.
"In future oil demand will grow, most of the demand will be for fossil fuel and most of it will come from the Middle East," he said.

"The Middle East countries will gain the largest portion of incremental supplies due to their large resource base and low development costs. Middle East oil producers will have a pivotal role in the world's oil markets by 2010."
Ismail said that increasing taxation imposed by consuming countries could render OPEC members unable to raise the required investment for future capacity expansion.

"The net earnings per barrel of most consuming nations are already several times higher than those collected by OPEC member countries," said Ismail. "Extra tax-take by consumer governments will lead to the reduction in the demand in future and discourage OPEC and other non-OPEC producers from investment in expanding output capacity due to future oil demand."
